The fundamental struck is low and distant, with rich layers of overtones. Different striking points and forces give widely varied results, from a soft low hum to a clear high note. The sound resonates strongly and echoes and lingers in the space. In an ensemble the agong's timbre effectively adds a national atmosphere and rhythmic force to the whole.
A鑼（Agong，Hornbostel–Sachs 111.241.2）屬體鳴樂: The agong (Hornbostel–Sachs 111.241.2) is an idiophone, common in the traditional music of the Philippines and Indonesia. It usually takes the form of two large gongs hung vertically, and in the kulintang ensemble it provides a supporting rhythm alongside the babandil gong, the gandingan gongs and the dabakan drum; among the Maguindanao, Maranao, Sama Bajau and Tausug peoples it also appears in the agung orchestra. The source also mentions that it can be used in solo competitions and for signalling, but the only specific pieces given are the tagunggo section and the tidto rhythm pattern.
演奏者通常站立於樂器旁，左手以拇指與其餘手指夾持上緣鑼框，右手持短槌敲擊中央凸鈕: The player usually stands beside the instrument, gripping the top of the gong frame with the thumb and fingers of the left hand while striking the central boss with a short beater in the right. After it sounds, the hand, knee or beater head can be pressed against the boss to damp it. A beginner can practise single-beater strokes and damping first, then the division of work between the two gongs: the lower gong on the right falls mostly on the strong beats, the higher gong on the left mostly on the weak beats, making a counterpoint with the melody. If one person plays, the higher gong can be turned to face the player and the lower gong held steady at an angle by an assistant; or only the higher gong may be struck. Techniques using two beaters or a reversed note order also exist, mostly for competitions and performances.

The beater is a short wooden stick with one end wrapped in a soft but tough material such as rubber. The gongs are hung on rope and fixed to a branch, a roof beam, a ceiling or a gong stand. Beyond the metal, the wooden stick, the wrapping and the rope, the source does not state the materials of the other parts.
阿貢鑼（Agong，Hornbostel–Sachs 111.241.2）屬體鳴: The agong (Hornbostel–Sachs 111.241.2) is an idiophone whose origin is connected with Indonesia; the name comes from Malay agong and Indonesian/Javanese ageng. In the 1770s the British explorer Thomas Forrest recorded that the people of the Philippines prized round-bossed gongs from Cilegon in Java. It later became a supporting instrument of the kulintang ensemble among the Maguindanao, Maranao, Sama Bajau and Tausug of the Philippines, and spread to Palawan, Panay, Mindoro, Mindanao, Sabah, Sulawesi, Sarawak and Kalimantan, forming part of the agong ensemble.

The agong (also called agung) is a set of two wide-rimmed, vertically hung idiophone gongs, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.241.2. It resembles a pot gong, hung on ropes near waist height; the player stands, steadying the frame with one hand and striking the central boss with a soft-padded short beater in the other, and can damp the sound with hand, knee or beater head. It is found mainly among the Maguindanao, Maranao, Sama-Bajau and Tausug of the Philippines, where it takes the supporting part in the gandingan ensemble, and is also used in the agong ensembles of Sabah, Sulawesi, Sarawak and Kalimantan.
